title: Backtracking-weighted PageRank is not coordinatewise monotone: minimal counterexamples, a certified census and endpoint tests
shortTitle: Turning up backtracking can move PageRank both ways
oneLine: As a PageRank walker's weight for stepping straight back is turned up, a vertex score can fall and then rise again, so two cheap scores cannot tell which side the expensive non-backtracking score lies on; a five-vertex house graph refutes Conjectures 3.1 and 3.2 of Glover, Jones, Kempton and Oveson (2026).
abstract: PageRank scores the vertices of a network by a random walk that occasionally restarts. A walk with memory can weight an immediate return along the edge just used by a parameter μ: μ = 0 forbids returns (non-backtracking PageRank), μ = 1 is ordinary PageRank and μ → ∞ makes the walk bounce on one edge, where the score has a cheap closed form. Glover, Jones, Kempton and Oveson (Applied Mathematics and Computation, 2026; arXiv:2211.13353v2) conjectured that every vertex score is monotone in μ and that the spread of scores is monotone too; if true, the ordinary and infinite-backtracking scores would show which side of ordinary PageRank the non-backtracking score lies on. This candidate shows that both clauses of their Conjecture 3.1 fail. On the five-vertex house graph with uniform restart and damping ε = 1/2, the roof vertex has π₀ = 638/3615, π₁ = 22/125 and π∞ = 8/45: both endpoints lie above the middle value, so the score dips and recovers and the shortcut points the wrong way. An exact cubic formula classifies every damping value: the roof is monotone exactly when ε ≤ ε_c ≈ 0.2407. Among graphs of minimum degree two, five vertices is the smallest order for every damping value (the house and the gem); with leaves allowed the four-vertex paw already fails for ε in (0, ε₁) ∪ (ε₂, 1), where four is then the smallest order, and even a five-vertex tree fails. A certified exact census of all 995 connected graphs on two to seven vertices, at five damping values, finds a nonmonotone vertex in 675 of the 853 seven-vertex graphs for some listed damping value. Both readings of the spread clause also fail, even when the extreme vertices are unique. A two-step criterion explains which vertices dip at small damping, and an exact slope formula at ordinary PageRank gives cheap sufficient tests. Exact invariance under backtracking holds if and only if P²v = v, and the degree-tail Conjecture 3.2 fails, in its local-weak-convergence reading, for every tail index above one. Numerical experiments find 10–41% of vertices nonmonotone on standard networks, with small excursions and stable rankings. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Three-number certificate: on the house graph with uniform restart and ε = 1/2, the roof vertex has π₀ = 638/3615, π₁ = 22/125 and π∞ = 8/45; both endpoints exceed the middle value, so the score is not monotone in μ and the endpoint shortcut points the wrong way (exact).

House classification: the roof response is an explicit ratio of cubics in μ; it is monotone if and only if ε ≤ ε_c ≈ 0.2406813, otherwise it has exactly one strict minimum, located at μ = 1 if and only if ε = 4/9; the shortcut gives the wrong side if and only if ε > ε_0 ≈ 0.3291038 (Theorems 3.1, 4.1, Proposition 4.3, proof).

Smallest counterexamples: with minimum degree at least two, order five is minimal for every ε in (0, 1), witnessed by the house for ε > ε_c and the gem for ε ≤ 1/3; with leaves allowed the four-vertex paw fails exactly for ε in (0, ε₁) ∪ (ε₂, 1), ε₁ ≈ 0.078, ε₂ ≈ 0.436, so the smallest order is four there and five on [ε₁, ε₂]; covers lift failures to every order 5k (Theorem 5.2, Proposition 5.3, Corollary 5.4, Corollary 5.7, proof).
A five-vertex tree has a leaf that decreases and then increases for μ inside (0, 1) at ε = 1/2, so trees are not always monotone (Proposition 5.5, exact certificate).

Certified census of all 995 connected graphs on two to seven vertices at five damping values: 675 of 853 seven-vertex graphs, and 353 of 507 of minimum degree two, have a nonmonotone vertex for some listed ε; the census says nothing between the five listed values (certified exact computation).

Cheap partial substitute: a small-damping two-step criterion and an exact formula for dπ/dμ at μ = 1 give three sufficient endpoint tests; at ε = 1/2 they detect 285 of the 478 nonmonotone census vertices of minimum degree two (proof; exact check).

Both readings of the spread clause fail, and the spread can increase even when the extreme vertices are unique for every μ (Propositions 8.1–8.2, exact certificates); scores are exactly μ-independent if and only if P²v = v (Theorem 9.1, proof); the degree-tail Conjecture 3.2 fails for every tail index α > 1 in its local-weak-convergence reading (Theorem 11.2, proof).
On standard networks 10–41% of vertices are nonmonotone, excursions are small and rankings are stable (numerical).

narration: Turning up backtracking can move PageRank both ways. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the background. PageRank ranks the points of a network by how often a random walker visits them, as it follows links and sometimes restarts. Backtracking means stepping straight back along the link just used. Ordinary PageRank treats it like any other step. Forbidding it gives non-backtracking PageRank, which is costly to compute. Unlimited backtracking, where the walker bounces on one link, is cheap. Next, the conjecture. In 2026, Glover, Jones, Kempton and Oveson conjectured that, as backtracking is made more likely, every score moves in one direction only. That would give a shortcut: comparing the ordinary score with the cheap extreme would show which side the costly one lies on. Now, the main finding. The conjecture is false. On the house graph, a square with a triangular roof, call the roof scores pi sub zero with no backtracking, pi sub one for ordinary PageRank, and pi sub infinity for unlimited backtracking. When the walker follows a link half the time, they are exactly 638 over 3615, 22 over 125, and 8 over 45. Both ends lie above the middle, so the score dips and recovers, and the shortcut points the wrong way. Five points is the smallest example without dead ends, and an exact census finds failures in most seven-point networks. A second conjecture, about degree tails, also fails. How sure is this? The main results are proved, and the census is certified in exact arithmetic. Tests on real networks are numerical only, and there the dips are small. Finally, the limits. The census covers five restart rates only, and no proof assistant was used. The conjecture's wording was checked against arXiv only, as the journal version was inaccessible. One question about random networks remains open. It is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate, with AI-assisted adversarial review only, not peer review. Published on 23 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: An exact three-value certificate on the five-vertex house graph (π₀ = 638/3615, π₁ = 22/125, π∞ = 8/45 at ε = 1/2) refutes the coordinatewise clause of Conjecture 3.1 of Glover, Jones, Kempton and Oveson (2026); exact certificates refute both readings of its spread clause (also with unique extreme vertices), and a clique-chain construction refutes Conjecture 3.2 for every tail index α > 1.
decisionObject.scope: The backtracking-weighted edge-lift PageRank of the source (tail projection, column-stochastic reading) on finite connected simple undirected graphs, with the continuous leaf extension; uniform restart unless stated. The census is certified at five damping values only; prevalence figures are numerical; Conjecture 3.2 is refuted under a local-weak-convergence reading and any reading that requires unbounded scores; the configuration-model tail transfer is open.
